title: “那是相当煎熬的三个月”——Undead Labs 负责人 Philip Holt 谈 Xbox 剥离工作室后发生了什么
content:
"It was a pretty harrowing three months" – Undead Labs head Philip Holt on what happened after Xbox cut the studio loose | GamesIndustry.biz

.
Back in July, Xbox announced plans to
divest five studios
. Among them was State of Decay maker Undead Labs, which Microsoft had acquired back in 2018.
Undead Labs CEO Philip Holt tells
GamesIndustry.biz
that he had a small amount of warning before the public announcement, but it still came as a shock. It led to a "deeply unsettling" atmosphere for the employees at the studio, who dwelt on the "fear of what would happen if we all became unemployed," says Holt, as well as worrying they might not have a chance to ship State of Decay 3, a game they've been working on for years.
Philip Holt  |
Image credit:
Undead Labs
To take away some of the uncertainty, he made a decision to be fully transparent with Undead's employees about what was happening with the studio in the months that followed. "There was a period of time where it was a weekly update to the whole company," he says, adding that he had some "pretty direct and candid conversations" with employees. "I think it settled people down, and I think it strengthened the bonds of trust that we have with each other."
At first, there was hope of securing a buyer. "I think initially Microsoft was interested in finding an acquirer for the studio, and that could have been a great outcome for us," says Holt. "I also believed that, because we were so close to shipping the game, we could put together an offer that would be pretty credible, and it would allow the employees to control and own the company."
"So yes, we talked to investors, both Microsoft shopping the studio and us, not necessarily looking for a buyer, but looking for an investor to come in with cash. But because we're pre-revenue, I think a lot of those investors were really looking for control of a company, a majority position, and then I'm working for a financier. So we shifted gears to looking for publishing money."
That was slightly easier to come by, although not by much. "There was a period where I was almost like, if State of Decay 3 can't find its way to finishing, there's something really deeply wrong with the industry," says Holt. "But that was not a very helpful frame to hold, so I didn't hold it for very long."
"I was almost like, if State of Decay 3 can't find its way to finishing, there's something really deeply wrong with the industry"
It helped that State of Decay 3 is so close to launch, currently with a 2027 release window. The studio was eventually able to land an agreement with an as-yet-unnamed publisher for the game. "And so between the cash balance that we had on hand and publishing money, we're able to finish the game on our own without any investors coming in," says Holt. "We have taken no outside investors, which I think is pretty remarkable, honestly."
Most importantly, Undead Labs is
now employee-owned
. "It's so rare, I think, to be in a spot where the creators have commercial and operational control of their own business and it could be rewarded by the success or failure of their work," he says. "We're just so grateful to be in that spot."
But getting here has taken an almighty effort. "It's a serious act of will to navigate a path to an outcome like this. It was a pretty harrowing three months."
Undead 2.0
In terms of the corporate structure of the newly independent firm, Holt says they registered a new company  – "basically a Delaware C corporation" – which then acquired Undead Labs, and now they  are in the process of issuing equity to all employees of the company.
He stresses the importance of employees owning shares in the firm. "I think it increases the motivation. It makes the realities of the economics of the industry just more present in daily work. People are working for themselves. They're not really working for a taskmaster that sits somewhere else."
State of Decay 3 is set for release in 2027  |
Image credit:
Undead Labs
Some employees own more shares than others, something that Holt says is determined by "a lot of factors". But he says he doesn't have a majority stake. "It is typical that a CEO owns a majority equity in the company. I didn't want to be a majority owner, but I did want to have control. So we created multiple classes of stock that allow for super voting rights, so I can be in a minority ownership position and still have voting control of the company."
The bonus of this is that there are more shares to go around for everyone else, so Undead can be "more generous in the equity distribution that we can do with our employees," Holt says.
"You can't command commitment. You earn it, you can only earn it"
There's not much employees can do with those shares right now, other than sell them back to the company – but Holt notes that if someone ever bought the firm, the employees would be due for a windfall. And there might be the possibility of dividends in the future. "If we were generating enough profit that we wanted to return some of it to employees, that would be a good way to do it," says Holt. "Thinking through the economic rewards of making a great game that is attached to a big audience and returning that to the creators of the game itself – I'm just so grateful to be in a spot where we're able to do that."
Above all though, he thinks the new structure is an excellent motivator. "Great games are made by teams that are absolutely dedicated, committed to the game itself. You can't command commitment. You earn it, you can only earn it. And I think once I made that realisation, I realised that that becomes the objective of the corporation itself – to earn the commitment of the employees in service of the game that we're making."
Downsizing
